question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate word. Choose the correct alternative.
His heart pounded as he checked his rearview mirror and saw only the dark _______ of highway.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. stretch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Stretch" here means a continuous area or expanse (of road, land, water, etc.) — used with a road, this means an extended, unbroken length of highway visible ahead in the dark.
◦ Example: We drove along a lonely stretch of highway for hours.

• The sentence describes fear/tension while driving at night, so the blank must be a word that naturally collocates with "highway", describing a length of road rather than an abstract quality.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Vitality" means "energy, liveliness"; it cannot describe a length of road, so it does not fit the context.

• Option 3: "Trench" means "a long, narrow ditch dug in the ground"; while it is a physical feature, it does not collocate with "of highway" and is not what one would see in a rearview mirror while driving.

• Option 4: "Emancipation" means "freedom from restriction or oppression"; it is entirely unrelated to a physical road and makes no sense in the sentence.

NOTE

• Learn common collocations with "stretch": a stretch of road/water/land/time, "for a long stretch", "the home stretch".

• Do not confuse "stretch" (a noun meaning expanse) with "stretch" as a verb (to extend physically) — context decides the correct sense.

question:
The question below consists of a set of labeled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Within an hour, he was in jail.
Q. He made no attempts to hide his identity and even looked directly into the security camera and smiled.
R. On Jan 6, 1995, McArthur Wheeler boldly robbed two banks in broad daylight with no disguise.
S. By 11:00 at night, his picture was all over the news, leading an informant to identify Wheeler to the police.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. RQSP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence R logically opens the paragraph, introducing the subject and setting the scene: "On Jan 6, 1995, McArthur Wheeler boldly robbed two banks in broad daylight with no disguise."

• Sentence Q follows R, adding a detail about his behaviour immediately during/after the robbery: "He made no attempts to hide his identity and even looked directly into the security camera and smiled."

• Sentence S follows next, describing the consequence of that behaviour: "By 11:00 at night, his picture was all over the news, leading an informant to identify Wheeler to the police."

• Sentence P concludes the paragraph with the final outcome: "Within an hour, he was in jail."

Rule — Parajumble sequencing: Identify the sentence that introduces the subject/topic (usually containing a proper noun or setting the scene) as the opening sentence, then arrange the remaining sentences in chronological/cause-effect order.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (RPSQ) is incorrect because it places P (he was in jail) immediately after R, before explaining how he was caught (Q and S), breaking the cause-effect chain.

• Option 2 (SPQR) is incorrect because it begins with S, which uses the pronoun "his" without first establishing who "he" is — R must come first to introduce Wheeler.

• Option 4 (PRQS) is incorrect for the same reason — it starts with the conclusion (P) before the subject has even been introduced.

NOTE

• In parajumbles, always look for the sentence that introduces a name/subject for the first time — it is almost always the opening sentence.

• Pronouns (he, his, it, this) appearing in a sentence indicate that sentence cannot be the first sentence, since the noun they refer to must already be established.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Isn't knowledge supposed to make life sweeter and happier?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Wisdom.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "Knowledge" means information, understanding, or facts acquired through experience, study, or awareness. (ज्ञान)

• Among the given options, "Wisdom" is the closest in meaning — it also refers to the possession of knowledge, understanding, and good judgement. (बुद्धि/ज्ञान)
◦ Example: With age comes knowledge, and hopefully, wisdom as well.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Curriculum" (पाठ्यक्रम) means the subjects/courses taught in a school or college — a specific, structured set of studies, not general knowledge.

• Option 2: "Profession" (पेशा) means an occupation involving specialised training, such as law or medicine — unrelated to the meaning of "knowledge".

• Option 4: "Superiority" (श्रेष्ठता) means the state of being better or higher in status — it does not mean knowledge or awareness.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Knowledge": wisdom, awareness, understanding, erudition, learning, insight.

• Do not confuse "knowledge" (facts/information) with "intelligence" (the ability to acquire and apply knowledge) — SSC often tests this distinction.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The man which was present at the meeting spoke against the chairperson.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The man who was present.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The relative pronoun "which" is used only for animals and things, never for persons. Since "the man" is a person, the correct relative pronoun is "who".

• Rule — Relative Pronouns: "Who"/"whom" is used for persons; "which" is used for animals and things; "that" can be used for both persons and things in restrictive clauses.

• The subject "the man" performs the action "was present", so the subject relative pronoun "who" (not the object form "whom") is required.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The man which were present" is incorrect on two counts — "which" cannot refer to a person, and "were" wrongly uses a plural verb with the singular subject "the man".

• Option 2: "The men which was present" is incorrect because "which" is used for a person, "men" (plural) does not agree with "was" (singular), and changing "man" to "men" alters the meaning.

• Option 3: "The man whom was present" is incorrect because "whom" is the objective case of "who" and cannot be used as the subject of the verb "was".

NOTE

• "Whom" is used only when the pronoun is the object of a verb or preposition, e.g., "The man whom I met was a doctor."

• Common error type in SSC: examine whether the relative pronoun refers to a person, animal, or thing before choosing who/which/whom.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to complete the given sentence.
They were not able to get the item from the store because it was __________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. out of stock.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "out of stock" means not currently available for purchase because the supply has been used up or exhausted. (स्टॉक में न होना/समाप्त हो जाना)
◦ Example: The bakery had run out of bread, so the popular loaf was out of stock.

• Since the sentence says "they were not able to get the item from the store", the reason must relate to the unavailability of the item, which "out of stock" expresses exactly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "In fashion" (प्रचलन में) means "currently popular or stylish" — unrelated to being unable to buy an item.

• Option 2: "In vain" (व्यर्थ) means "without success or result"; it describes an unsuccessful action, not the state of an item being unavailable in a store.

• Option 4: "On leave" (छुट्टी पर) means "away from work temporarily", used for people, not for items in a store.

NOTE

• Related phrases: "in stock" (available for sale), "sold out" (completely sold), "back-order" (ordered but not yet available).

• Distinguish "in vain" (used for a failed effort) from "out of stock" (used for unavailable goods) — SSC frequently mixes such phrases as distractors.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.
I must tell you that it all went pear-shaped after you left the meeting in the middle.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Went terribly wrong.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Went pear-shaped" means to go badly wrong; to fail or turn out disastrously despite going well earlier. (बुरी तरह बिगड़ जाना)
◦ Example: The plan was going smoothly until the weather changed, and then everything went pear-shaped.

• The idiom likely originates from pilot slang, where an attempted perfect circular flying loop that failed to form correctly ended up looking like a "pear" shape instead.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Became very entertaining" is incorrect — the idiom carries a strongly negative meaning of failure, not enjoyment.

• Option 3: "Became tragic" is incorrect — while negative, "tragic" implies sorrow/grief, whereas "went pear-shaped" simply means something went wrong or failed, without necessarily implying tragedy.

• Option 4: "Turned out fine" is incorrect — this is the opposite meaning; "went pear-shaped" specifically means the opposite of a good outcome.

NOTE

• Other idioms of failure/going wrong often asked in SSC: "go belly up" (fail completely, especially a business), "go south" (decline or fail), "go haywire" (go out of control), "go awry" (go wrong).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'dwindle' in the sentence given below.
Rahul advised Neerja to appreciate or motivate her younger brother and not to dwindle or neglect his ideas all the time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. complement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dwindle" means to become gradually smaller or weaker; to diminish, decline, or belittle something. (धीरे-धीरे कम होना/घटाना)

• In the sentence, Rahul advises Neerja "to appreciate or motivate" her brother, and NOT "to dwindle or neglect" his ideas — here "dwindle" is used to mean diminishing or undervaluing the worth of his ideas.

• "Complement" means to add to something in a way that enhances, completes, or improves it. (पूरक बनकर मूल्य बढ़ाना) This conveys the sense of adding value — the direct opposite of diminishing or reducing value, which is exactly what "dwindle" means here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Deprecate" means "to express disapproval of, or to play down the importance of" — this is close in meaning to "dwindle" as used here, making it a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Motivate" already occurs in the given sentence itself as the word contrasted with "dwindle/neglect"; being a word already present in the sentence, it is a distractor and not the intended antonym option.

• Option 4: "Neglect" is paired with "dwindle" in the sentence as another undesirable action (both mean to disregard/diminish), so it is a synonym of "dwindle", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Antonym pairs to remember: dwindle × augment/increase/enhance/complement; deprecate × appreciate/praise; neglect × attend to/cherish.

• In antonym questions, first eliminate any option that is a synonym of the given word — here "deprecate" and "neglect" are both close to "dwindle" in meaning and can be ruled out immediately.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The bus is now full of passengers, it will leave soon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. is going to leave.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence gives visible present evidence ("The bus is now full of passengers") for a prediction about the near future ("it will leave soon") — this is the classic context for the "going to" future, used to predict something based on present evidence.

• Rule — "Going to" Future: Subject + is/am/are + going to + V1, used for (i) a prediction based on present evidence/signs, and (ii) a plan or intention already decided before the moment of speaking.

• Since the bus being full is present evidence that it is about to depart, "is going to leave" is the most appropriate substitute for "will leave".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "leaves" (simple present) is used for habitual/scheduled actions (e.g., timetables), not for a prediction drawn from the present situation of the bus being full.

• Option 2: "is leaving" (present continuous) is generally used for a fixed arrangement/plan (e.g., "I am leaving tomorrow at 5 pm"), not for a spontaneous prediction based on present evidence.

• Option 4: "has to leave" expresses obligation/necessity ("must leave"), which changes the meaning of the sentence — the original expresses a prediction, not an obligation.

NOTE

• "Will" is used for instant decisions, promises, and general predictions without present evidence; "going to" is used specifically for predictions backed by present evidence, and for pre-decided plans.

• Commonly confused future forms in SSC: will vs going to vs present continuous (for fixed plans) vs simple present (for timetables/schedules).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Where was this pen found by him?
option_1: Where do he find this pen?
option_2: Where does he find this pen?
option_3: Where did he found this pen?
option_4: Where did he find this pen?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Where did he find this pen?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Where was this pen found by him?" is a passive interrogative sentence in the Simple Past Tense (was + V3 + by + subject, with a question word).

• Rule — Passive to Active (Simple Past, Wh-question): Passive: Wh-word + was/were + Object + V3 + by + Subject? → Active: Wh-word + did + Subject + V1 + Object?

• Applying the rule: the agent "by him" becomes the subject "he"; the passive verb "was found" becomes "did find" (auxiliary "did" + base form "find"); and the subject of the passive "this pen" becomes the object.
◦ Active: Where did he find this pen?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Where do he find this pen?" is incorrect — it wrongly uses the simple present auxiliary "do" (also disagreeing with "he", which needs "does") instead of the simple past "did" required by the original past tense sentence.

• Option 2: "Where does he find this pen?" is incorrect — "does" makes the sentence simple present, changing the tense of the original passive sentence, which was in the simple past.

• Option 3: "Where did he found this pen?" is incorrect — after the auxiliary "did", the main verb must be in its base form ("find"), not the past form ("found").

NOTE

• Rule: after "did" in a question or negative sentence, always use the base form (V1) of the verb, never the past form (V2).

• Passive-to-active conversion of "wh + by + agent" questions always shifts the agent into the subject position of the active sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
Kranthi loves to swim at the local swimming pool in order that relieve his work stress.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. in order to relieve.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "in order that relieve" is grammatically faulty — "in order that" must be followed by a full clause with a subject and a modal verb (e.g., "in order that he may/can relieve"), not directly by a bare verb.

• Rule — Expressing Purpose: "In order to + V1" (infinitive of purpose) is used to directly join a purpose to the main clause without a separate subject, when the subject of both clauses is the same. "In order that + subject + may/might/can/could + V1" is used when a full clause (with its own subject and modal) follows.

• Since no new subject or modal follows in the original sentence, the correct and concise construction is the infinitive of purpose: "in order to relieve".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in order which" is incorrect — "which" is a relative pronoun and cannot follow "in order" to express purpose.

• Option 2: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original phrase "in order that relieve" is grammatically wrong, as explained above — a substitution is required.

• Option 3: "in order as to relieve" is incorrect — "as" is redundant and not idiomatically used with "in order to"; the standard structure is simply "in order to + V1".

NOTE

• "So as to + V1" is another common infinitive-of-purpose construction similar to "in order to + V1", used when the subject remains the same in both clauses.

• Remember: "in order that" is always followed by a clause containing a modal verb (may/might/can/could/will/shall), never directly by a bare infinitive.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Inherent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. extraneous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Inherent" means existing as a natural, permanent, or essential part or quality of something; intrinsic. (अंतर्निहित/स्वाभाविक)

• "Extraneous" means coming from or existing outside; not essential or relevant; not a natural part of something. (बाहरी/असंगत) This is the direct opposite of "inherent".
◦ Example: The risk is inherent in the job, but the delays were due to extraneous factors like the weather.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Natural" is close in meaning to "inherent" itself (both suggest something that exists as an essential quality), making it a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Induce" means "to persuade or bring about"; it is unrelated in meaning to "inherent" and does not form a natural antonym pair with it.

• Option 4: "Restricted" means "limited or controlled"; it describes a constraint, not the opposite of something being an essential/natural quality.

NOTE

• Antonym pairs to remember: inherent × extraneous/acquired/external; intrinsic × extrinsic.

• Do not confuse "inherent" (an essential built-in quality) with "inherited" (passed down from parents/ancestors) — SSC often uses these as distractors of each other.

question:
Select the idiom from the given options that gives the most appropriate meaning of the highlighted text in the following sentence.
A village fair is a place that contains many interesting objects. People of all age groups eagerly wait for this.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Aladdin's cave.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Aladdin's cave" means a place full of an impressive number of wonderful or valuable things. (अनगिनत आकर्षक चीज़ों से भरी जगह)
◦ Example: The old attic was like an Aladdin's cave, full of antiques and forgotten treasures.

• The idiom comes from the folk tale of Aladdin, who discovers a magical cave filled with treasure. A village fair, described as "a place that contains many interesting objects" that people of all ages "eagerly wait for", matches this meaning exactly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Road to Damascus" means "a sudden and dramatic moment of realization or conversion", unrelated to a place full of interesting objects.

• Option 2: "Ivory tower" means "a state of being detached from the practical realities of everyday life", often used for academics/intellectuals — it does not mean a place of many interesting things.

• Option 4: "Jewel in the crown" means "the best or most valuable part of something", referring to a single prized item or achievement, not a place containing many varied interesting objects.

NOTE

• Other idioms describing a place full of good/valuable things: "a treasure trove" (a place or collection full of valuable things), "a gold mine" (a great source of something valuable).

• Do not confuse "Aladdin's cave" (many valuable/interesting things) with "Pandora's box" (a source of many unforeseen troubles) — both involve a container in folklore but have opposite connotations.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
I named the child Ritesh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The child was named Ritesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "I named the child Ritesh" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense, with "the child" as the direct object and "Ritesh" as the object complement.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense: Active: Subject + V2 + Object; Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + (by + Subject). When the subject of the active sentence is a generic/unimportant "I", the agent "by me" is usually dropped in the passive.

• Applying the rule: the object "the child" becomes the subject; the verb "named" (V2) becomes "was named" (V3, since "child" is singular); and the object complement "Ritesh" remains after the verb.
◦ Passive: The child was named Ritesh.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "The child Ritesh is named." is incorrect — it wrongly uses the simple present tense ("is named") instead of the simple past, and it incorrectly attaches "Ritesh" to "child" as if it were already his name before the naming took place.

• Option 3: "The child is named Ritesh." is incorrect for the same reason — "is named" is present tense, which does not match the past tense of the original active sentence "named".

• Option 4: "The child Ritesh was named." is incorrect — it wrongly places "Ritesh" immediately after "child" as an existing name, dropping the object complement structure and distorting the original meaning (in the original, the child is NAMED "Ritesh" as a result of the naming, not already called that).

NOTE

• When a verb takes both a direct object and an object complement (e.g., name, call, elect, appoint), the passive keeps the object complement immediately after the passive verb: Object + was/were + V3 + Complement.

• The agent ("by me"/"by I") is typically omitted in the passive when it is obvious, unimportant, or refers to "I"/"we" in a general statement.

question: Select the sentences that contains no spelling errors in the given context.
option_1: Furrow from the protestors was heard outside the president's house.
option_2: Furoroe from the protestors was heard outside the president's house.
option_3: Furore from the protestors was heard outside the president's house.
option_4: Furorow from the protestors was heard outside the president's house.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Furore from the protestors was heard outside the president's house.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Furore" — a noun meaning "an outbreak of public anger or excitement".
◦ Example: The minister's remark caused a furore across the country.

• Spelling key: F-U-R-O-R-E. The word ends in "-ore" (rhyming with "before"), with a single "r", then "o", then another single "r" before the final "e".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Furrow" is a different, existing word here that is incorrect in this context — it actually means "a long narrow trench made by a plough", not an outcry of public anger.

• Option 2: "Furoroe" is incorrect — the letters have been jumbled; it wrongly repeats "or" and misplaces the "o".

• Option 4: "Furorow" is incorrect — it wrongly adds an extra "ow" at the end, which does not exist in the correct spelling "furore".

NOTE

• "Furore" (British spelling) is spelt "furor" in American English, without the final "e".

• Do not confuse "furore" (public outcry/anger) with "furrow" (a groove cut by a plough) — they look and sound similar but have completely different meanings.

question:
In the given sentence, one word may have been incorrectly spelt. Select the correctly spelt word from the given alternatives. If there is no error, select 'No error' as your answer.
Decades of enimity between Lomovs and Chubukovs came to an end with the marriage between the two families.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. enmity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "enimity" in the given sentence is misspelt. The correct spelling is "enmity", meaning "a state or feeling of active hostility or ill will".
◦ Example: Years of enmity between the two families ended when their children got married.

• Spelling key: E-N-M-I-T-Y. There is no extra "i" between "en" and "mity" — the letter "m" follows "en" directly, i.e., EN + MITY.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "enemity" is incorrect — it wrongly inserts an extra "e" (making it look like "enemy" + "ity"), which is not the correct spelling.

• Option 3: "anaemity" is incorrect and not even a real word — it confuses the spelling with "anaemia" (a medical condition), which is unrelated in meaning and spelling.

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because "enimity" as printed in the original sentence is indeed misspelt, as explained above.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "enmity" (hostility) with "amity" (friendship) — they are near-opposite in meaning but similar in spelling/sound.

• Other commonly misspelt SSC words with silent/tricky vowels: "questionnaire", "perseverance", "maintenance", "liaison".

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
She tells me that I am her lucky charm.
option_1: She says to me, “You was my lucky charm.”
option_2: She said to me, “You are lucky charm.”
option_3: She says to me, “I am your lucky charm.”
option_4: She says to me, “You are my lucky charm.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. She says to me, "You are my lucky charm."

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The reporting verb "tells" is in the Simple Present Tense, so there is NO backshift of tense while converting to direct speech — the tense inside the quotation marks stays exactly as it is in the indirect sentence.

• Rule — Indirect to Direct Speech: Reporting verb "tell(s)/told + object" → "say(s)/said to + object" in direct speech; the pronoun "I" (referring to the listener "me" in the indirect sentence) is converted to "you"; the possessive "her" (referring to the speaker) is converted to "my".

• Applying the rule: "tells me" → "says to me"; "that" is dropped and quotation marks are added; "I am her lucky charm" → "You are my lucky charm" (since "I" refers to the person being told, i.e. "you", and "her" refers to the speaker herself, i.e. "my").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: 'She says to me, "You was my lucky charm."' is incorrect — "was" is grammatically wrong with "you"; since the reporting verb is present tense, no backshift is needed and the correct verb is "are".

• Option 2: 'She said to me, "You are lucky charm."' is incorrect — it wrongly changes the reporting verb to "said" (past tense), which is not supported by the given sentence ("tells", present tense), and it also drops the possessive "my" before "lucky charm".

• Option 3: 'She says to me, "I am your lucky charm."' is incorrect — it fails to convert the pronouns correctly; "I" in the indirect sentence refers to the listener, so it must become "you" in direct speech, not remain "I".

NOTE

• When the reporting verb is in the Simple Present or Simple Future tense, the tense of the verb inside the direct speech does NOT change (no backshift rule applies).

• Pronoun conversion is the most common error area: always ask "who does 'I', 'you', 'my', 'her' refer to?" before converting between direct and indirect speech.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Chide
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Scold.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Chide" means to express disapproval or reprimand someone, typically in a mild or gentle way; to scold. (डांटना/फटकारना)
◦ Example: The teacher chided the students for arriving late to class.

• "Scold" also means "to rebuke or criticise someone angrily for a fault or misbehaviour", making it the closest match in meaning to "chide".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Prevent" (रोकना) means "to stop something from happening"; it does not involve any element of reprimanding or scolding.

• Option 2: "Rescue" (बचाना) means "to save someone from danger or harm"; it is unrelated to the act of expressing disapproval.

• Option 4: "Follow" (अनुसरण करना) means "to come after or obey"; it has no connection to reprimanding someone.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "chide": rebuke, reprimand, reproach, admonish, scold, upbraid.

• Do not confuse "chide" (mild scolding) with words that sound similar like "chase" or "cheat" — focus on the exact spelling and root meaning in vocabulary questions.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The boy, as well as / his friends, were / absent from the class / when the teacher came.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. his friends, were.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "The boy", which is singular; the phrase "as well as his friends" is a parenthetical phrase (not a joint subject with "and") and does NOT make the subject plural.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "as well as": When two subjects are joined by "as well as" (also "along with", "together with", "in addition to"), the verb agrees only with the FIRST subject, not with the one after "as well as".

• Since "The boy" is singular, the verb must be the singular "was", not the plural "were" used in the segment "his friends, were".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "absent from the class" is grammatically correct and contains no error; it correctly follows the (corrected) verb.

• Option 2: "when the teacher came" is grammatically correct — a correctly formed subordinate clause in the simple past tense, matching the tense of the rest of the sentence.

• Option 4: "The boy, as well as" is grammatically correct as the start of the sentence — the subject "the boy" and the connecting phrase "as well as" are correctly used.

NOTE

• Phrases like "as well as", "along with", "together with", "in addition to", "besides", and "no less than" do NOT change the number of the verb — the verb always agrees with the main subject before these phrases.

• Contrast this with "and", which DOES combine two subjects into a plural subject requiring a plural verb (e.g., "The boy and his friends were absent").

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Genome-wide
P. with metabolites that influence
Q. traits like flavour, disease resistance and texture
R. analysis of each apple enabled
S. identification of genetic markers associated
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. RSPQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence R logically continues the opening phrase "Genome-wide" first, since it contains the main subject and verb: "analysis of each apple enabled..."

• Sentence S follows next, naming what was enabled: "...enabled identification of genetic markers associated..."

• Sentence P follows, specifying what the genetic markers are associated with: "...associated with metabolites that influence..."

• Sentence Q completes the sentence, naming what the metabolites influence: "...influence traits like flavour, disease resistance and texture."
◦ Full sentence: Genome-wide analysis of each apple enabled identification of genetic markers associated with metabolites that influence traits like flavour, disease resistance and texture.

Rule — Sentence-completion rearrangement: Read the fixed opening phrase carefully and identify which given part grammatically and logically continues it (usually the part with the main verb), then trace the chain of ideas (associated with → metabolites that influence → traits) to the end.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PQRS) is incorrect because it begins with "with metabolites that influence" immediately after "Genome-wide", which is grammatically broken and has no verb to complete the opening phrase.

• Option 2 (QRPS) is incorrect because it begins with "traits like flavour...", which cannot logically or grammatically follow "Genome-wide" directly.

• Option 4 (QRSP) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 — it does not begin with the sentence's main verb phrase (R), leaving "Genome-wide" without a grammatical continuation.

NOTE

• In sentence-completion rearrangement questions, first identify which segment contains the verb needed to complete the given opening fragment — that segment must come first.

• Then follow the logical chain of prepositions/relative clauses ("associated with... that influence...") to place the remaining segments correctly.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error.
He describes the place vivid / that inspired in us / a wish to visit / the same.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He describes the place vivid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "describes" is being modified — i.e., we are told HOW he describes the place — so an adverb is required, not an adjective.

• Rule: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, while adjectives modify only nouns/pronouns. Since "vivid" here is meant to describe the manner of the action "describes" (a verb), it must be changed to the adverb form "vividly".

• Correct segment: "He describes the place vividly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "the same." is grammatically correct as used here, referring back to "a wish to visit" (the place) without any error.

• Option 3: "a wish to visit" is grammatically correct — a correctly formed infinitive phrase functioning as the object.

• Option 4: "that inspired in us" is grammatically correct — a correctly formed relative clause modifying "a wish", using the simple past tense consistently with the rest of the sentence.

NOTE

• A common SSC error-spotting trap is an adjective used where an adverb is required (or vice versa) — always check whether the word modifies a noun (needs adjective) or a verb/adjective/adverb (needs adverb, usually formed by adding "-ly").

• Similar frequently tested pairs: quick/quickly, careful/carefully, bad/badly, real/really.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Exercise is the (1)_________ of muscles and limbs which is done to (2)______ a specific outcome. The chief aim of doing exercise is usually (3)_____ fitness. At the end of our (4)_____ day, we prefer to (5)_____ in leisure activities rather than a workout.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. movement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun describing what exercise IS — i.e., the physical action of muscles and limbs. "Movement" precisely means "an act of changing the physical location or position of the body or a part of it", which correctly defines what exercise is at its core.

• The sentence structure "Exercise is the ___ of muscles and limbs" needs a word that can define exercise in terms of muscles and limbs acting — "movement" fits this naturally (e.g., "movement of muscles").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Motion" is close in meaning to movement but is more commonly used for the movement of objects or mechanical/scientific motion (e.g., "laws of motion"), and does not collocate as naturally with "of muscles and limbs" as "movement" does.

• Option 2: "Current" means "a flow of water, air, or electricity", or "the general trend of ideas/events" — it does not describe the physical action of muscles and limbs.

• Option 4: "Fluctuation" means "an irregular rising and falling in number or amount", typically used for quantities like prices or temperature — it does not describe muscular activity.

NOTE

• "Movement" is the standard word used in fitness/exercise contexts to describe bodily action, e.g., "range of movement", "muscle movement".

• In cloze passages, always check which option best collocates with the surrounding words (here, "of muscles and limbs") rather than picking a word that is merely a loose synonym.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Exercise is the (1)_________ of muscles and limbs which is done to (2)______ a specific outcome. The chief aim of doing exercise is usually (3)_____ fitness. At the end of our (4)_____ day, we prefer to (5)_____ in leisure activities rather than a workout.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. attain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb meaning "to achieve or accomplish" a "specific outcome" — "attain" means exactly "to succeed in achieving something, usually after effort", which fits the sense of exercise being done with a purpose/goal.

• The sentence "which is done to ___ a specific outcome" needs a purpose-oriented verb of achievement; "attain a specific outcome" is a natural, idiomatic collocation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Yield" means "to produce or provide (a result, profit or crop)" or "to give way"; it does not fit the sense of purposefully working towards and achieving an outcome through exercise.

• Option 3: "Establish" means "to set up or create (an organisation, system, or fact) on a firm or permanent basis"; it does not naturally collocate with "a specific outcome" in the sense of a fitness goal.

• Option 4: "Procure" means "to obtain (something), typically with care or effort", generally used for acquiring objects or resources, not for achieving an abstract outcome like a fitness result.

NOTE

• "Attain" collocates naturally with goals/objectives/outcomes: attain a goal, attain success, attain fitness.

• Distinguish "attain" (achieve through effort) from "obtain" (get/acquire) and "procure" (obtain through deliberate effort, often formal/official) — all three are commonly confused in SSC cloze tests.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Exercise is the (1)_________ of muscles and limbs which is done to (2)______ a specific outcome. The chief aim of doing exercise is usually (3)_____ fitness. At the end of our (4)_____ day, we prefer to (5)_____ in leisure activities rather than a workout.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. enhancing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word that naturally collocates with "fitness" to describe the chief aim of exercise — "enhancing fitness" (i.e., improving or increasing one's level of fitness) is the standard, idiomatic phrase used in this context.

• "Enhance" means "to intensify, increase, or further improve the quality, value, or extent of something" — precisely the sense required when describing the aim of exercise with respect to fitness.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Magnifying" means "to make something appear larger than it is, or to exaggerate"; it is used for optical/exaggerated enlargement, not for improving a physical quality like fitness.

• Option 2: "Amplifying" means "to increase the volume/strength of a sound or signal, or to expand upon in speech/writing"; it does not naturally collocate with "fitness".

• Option 3: "Intensifying" means "to increase the strength, force, or degree of something"; while related in a general sense, it does not collocate as idiomatically with "fitness" as "enhancing" does — one does not typically say "intensify fitness".

NOTE

• Common exercise/health-related collocations: "enhance fitness", "improve stamina", "build strength", "boost immunity".

• "Enhance" is frequently tested in SSC cloze/vocabulary questions where the correct option must fit a specific, natural collocation, not just a loosely similar meaning.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Exercise is the (1)_________ of muscles and limbs which is done to (2)______ a specific outcome. The chief aim of doing exercise is usually (3)_____ fitness. At the end of our (4)_____ day, we prefer to (5)_____ in leisure activities rather than a workout.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. hectic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires an adjective describing "day" that explains why, at the end of it, people prefer leisure over a workout — i.e., the day must have been busy/tiring. "Hectic" means "full of incessant or frantic activity", the standard collocation with "day" in this context.
◦ Example: After a hectic day at work, she just wanted to relax on the couch.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Lively" means "full of energy, cheerful and animated"; it carries a positive connotation of enjoyable energy, not the sense of a tiring, busy day that leads someone to avoid a workout.

• Option 3: "Furious" means "extremely angry" (or, of activity, "very fast and uncontrolled"); it does not naturally describe a typical busy day and carries an inappropriate connotation of anger.

• Option 4: "Feverish" means "having or showing the symptoms of a fever" or "marked by intense/nervous excitement"; while it can suggest frantic activity, it is not the standard, natural collocation with "day" in this everyday context — "hectic day" is the idiomatic phrase.

NOTE

• Common collocations with "day": a hectic day, a busy day, a long day, a productive day — used to describe how demanding or tiring a day has been.

• "Hectic" is frequently tested in SSC vocabulary/cloze questions describing busy schedules, e.g., "a hectic schedule", "hectic pace of life".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Exercise is the (1)_________ of muscles and limbs which is done to (2)______ a specific outcome. The chief aim of doing exercise is usually (3)_____ fitness. At the end of our (4)_____ day, we prefer to (5)_____ in leisure activities rather than a workout.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. indulge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb that idiomatically takes the preposition "in" before an activity — "indulge in leisure activities" means "to allow oneself to enjoy the pleasure of" those activities, exactly the intended meaning of preferring to enjoy leisure activities rather than work out.
◦ Example: On weekends, he likes to indulge in his favourite hobby of painting.

• Rule — Verb + Preposition collocation: "Indulge" is idiomatically followed by "in" (indulge in something) when it means to allow oneself to enjoy something freely.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Luxuriate" means "to enjoy something as a luxury, to take great pleasure in something", and idiomatically takes "in" too ("luxuriate in"), but it more specifically implies enjoying comfort/relaxation (e.g., luxuriating in a warm bath) rather than generally engaging in leisure activities, making "indulge" the more natural and commonly tested fit here.

• Option 3: "Abandon" means "to give up completely or desert"; "abandon in leisure activities" is not idiomatic or meaningful — one cannot "abandon in" an activity.

• Option 4: "Coddle" means "to treat someone in an indulgent or overprotective way"; it is used for pampering another person, not for describing one's own engagement in leisure activities, and does not idiomatically take "in".

NOTE

• "Indulge in" + activity/hobby is a very common SSC collocation, e.g., "indulge in gossip", "indulge in shopping", "indulge in daydreaming".

• Distinguish "indulge" (allow oneself pleasure) from "indulge someone" (without "in" — to satisfy another person's wishes, often excessively).
